region: Capital city in Antigua and Barbuda
h1: Saint Johns travel, stays & events guide
heroText: St. John's is the compact capital of Antigua and Barbuda, built around a working harbour where cruise ships dock beside 18th-century warehouses. First-time visitors should climb the twin towers of the Cathedral of St John the Divine, browse restored buildings at Redcliffe Quay, and shop the waterfront stalls of Heritage Quay. V.C. Bird International Airport sits just northeast of the centre, making St. John's an easy gateway to Antigua's beaches and nearby English Harbour.

areas.name: Redcliffe Quay
areas.text: Redcliffe Quay is a restored 18th-century warehouse district turned dining and shopping strip, steps from the cruise port and cathedral.

areas.name: Heritage Quay
areas.text: Heritage Quay is St. John's main cruise terminal and duty-free shopping area, a busy base for short stays close to the harbour.

areas.name: Dickenson Bay
areas.text: Dickenson Bay is a beach hotel strip a short drive north of the centre, popular for calm water and sunset restaurants away from the harbour.

areas.name: Jolly Harbour
areas.text: Jolly Harbour is a marina community south of St. John's with villas, a golf course and a beach, suited to longer self-catering stays.

airports.name: V.C. Bird International Airport (ANU)
airports.search: V.C. Bird International Airport, St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda
airports.text: V.C. Bird International Airport sits about 8km northeast of St. John's; taxis meet every flight and the drive into town takes roughly 15-20 minutes.

stayOverview: Base in Redcliffe Quay or Heritage Quay for an easy first St. John's stay near the harbour, restaurants and cruise terminal, then compare Dickenson Bay for a beach hotel strip or Jolly Harbour for a marina setting with villas and golf a short drive from the centre.
hotelIntro: St. John's hotel choice comes down to setting: Redcliffe Quay and Heritage Quay suit short cruise stopovers and harbour-side dining, while Dickenson Bay offers a classic beach strip and Jolly Harbour suits families or longer stays wanting a marina and golf course nearby.
rentalCars: A rental car helps for reaching beaches like Dickenson Bay or day trips to English Harbour, though taxis cover the compact St. John's centre easily.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Stay in Redcliffe Quay or Heritage Quay for an easy first visit within walking distance of the harbour, cathedral and cruise terminal.

travelTips.title: Getting around
travelTips.text: Taxis and shared buses run between St. John's and the beaches; agree taxi fares before departure since meters are not standard.

travelTips.title: Cruise days
travelTips.text: Heritage Quay gets crowded when several cruise ships dock, so visit the cathedral and market early before the day-trip crowds arrive.

travelTips.title: Day trips
travelTips.text: Set aside half a day for Nelson's Dockyard and English Harbour on the south coast, one of the Caribbean's best-preserved Georgian naval sites.

highlights.title: Cathedral of St John the Divine
highlights.text: The Cathedral of St John the Divine's twin baroque towers dominate the skyline, rebuilt in stone after earthquakes destroyed earlier wooden churches.

highlights.title: Redcliffe Quay
highlights.text: Redcliffe Quay's restored 18th-century warehouses now hold boutiques, cafes and galleries, a pleasant walk from the cruise terminal at Heritage Quay.

highlights.title: Heritage Quay
highlights.text: Heritage Quay is the main cruise dock and duty-free shopping strip, busiest when ships are in port and quieter for an evening stroll.

highlights.title: Museum of Antigua and Barbuda
highlights.text: The Museum of Antigua and Barbuda, housed in the old courthouse, traces the island's Arawak, colonial and independence history in one compact gallery.

highlights.title: Fort James
highlights.text: Fort James guards the harbour entrance with 18th-century cannons and views over the water, a short taxi ride from the city centre.

highlights.title: Dickenson Bay
highlights.text: Dickenson Bay is the closest resort beach to St. John's, a calm stretch of sand lined with waterfront restaurants and watersports operators.

nearbyIdeas.name: Nelson's Dockyard
nearbyIdeas.label: Heritage
nearbyIdeas.text: Nelson's Dockyard is a restored Georgian naval dockyard on the south coast, a UNESCO World Heritage Site worth a half-day trip from St. John's.

nearbyIdeas.name: Betty's Hope
nearbyIdeas.label: Heritage
nearbyIdeas.text: Betty's Hope is a former sugar plantation with restored windmills, giving context on Antigua's colonial and enslaved history.

nearbyIdeas.name: Devil's Bridge
nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: Devil's Bridge is a natural limestone arch on the rugged east coast, carved by Atlantic waves crashing over the rock.

nearbyIdeas.name: Stingray City
nearbyIdeas.label: Island
nearbyIdeas.text: Stingray City is a shallow sandbar reef where boat trips let visitors wade among friendly southern stingrays.

history.text: John's was laid out following the French invasion of 1666, due to the site's strategic location on St.
An act was passed to build a town on the harbour in April 1668.
On 16 September 1675, a sitting of the island’s legislature in Old Road established six places of trade, one of which being St.
The plot caused a large scare, and in 1741, barracks were built on Rat Island, and in 1753, in the centre of the town.
In 1768, the city was hit by a major fire.
In 1772 the island was hit by a hurricane, resulting in significant damage to the city's shipping industry.
In 1782, the city was again damaged by a fire that occurred in one of the most densely populated parts of the city.
In 1784, the city's night watch was established, and citizens of the city were subjected to a tax to pay for it.
In 1786, another tax was established due to the prevalence of vermin, reptiles, prickly pear bushes lining the streets.
In 1790, the parish vestry was granted the ability to tax traders, which impacted the city due to it being the parish's economic centre.

history.label: 1800s
history.text: In the early 1800s, the present-day Government House was built.
John's was also the seat of government of the British Leeward Islands, a title it maintained until the colony's permanent abolishment in 1959.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: To prevent another fire, building regulations were also improved, with most public buildings being required to have brick walls and tiled or slate roofs.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: John's is the island's capital, the city is home to the Government Complex in the Botanical Gardens neighbourhood, which is home to the High Court, the Office of the Prime Minister, and the Parliament.
